sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Marzanna** ​(*marzanna*) — ‌Winter, Death, ‌Rebirth ​· Death ​goddess ​— belongs ​to the ​Slavic ‌tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Winter, ‌Death, ​Rebirth". The ‌name ​means "Death ​goddess"[^1].

**Marzanna** ​is ​the Slavic ​goddess of ‌winter, ​frost, and ‌death — ​the ‌withering power ​whose ‌departure is ​celebrated each ‌spring. ​Her name ​belongs to ‌the ‌cold family ‌of Polish ​*marznąć*, ​'to freeze,' ‌and ​her kinship ​with the ‌nightmare-hag ​*mora* ties ​her to ‌the ​dying of ‌the year ​itself. ​Every March ​her ​effigy is ‌drowned so ‌the ​world can ‌thaw.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records ​the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Marzanna** ‌and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/marzanna/). ​The ​displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a description ​computed from ​the ‌displayed form ​itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*marzanna* ​contains the ‌same letters: ​no ‌recovered diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives for ​this ​name; **Marzanna** ​is ​a ​scholarly transliteration ‌of ​the reconstructed ​spoken ‌form. Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"Death ‌goddess"[^1].

The ​canonical ​spelling **Marzanna** ​matches ​the conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. ​The plain ‌ASCII ​form *marzanna* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters, ​so no ‌lost ​diacritics or ​encoding ‌transition is ‌claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ​reviewed reference ‌spelling, ​preserve capitalization ​and ‌provenance, and ​keep ‌the original ​evidence ​visible. The ​displayed ​form is ‌ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a description ‌computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**marzanna** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Marzanna.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Marzanna" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Marzanna" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"marzanna" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Marzanna ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Marzanna ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Marzanna ‌place ​winter, death, ​rebirth ​at ​the center ​of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Marzanna ‌appears ​in slavic ‌tradition ​as ​winter, death, ​rebirth. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Death ​goddess", shapes ‌the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌Marzanna ​in ​ritual, text, ‌and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

‌The ​myths ​of Marzanna ​survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Marzanna ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Marzanna ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Slavic ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Marzanna, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​winter ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Most ​cultures personify ‌the good ‌seasons; the ​Slavs dared ​to personify ​the bad ​one. Marzanna ​is the ‌honest goddess: ​winter without ​apology, old ‌age and ​frost ‌and the ​failure of ‌things, given ​a woman's ​face and ​a woman's ​name. What ​her rite ‌teaches is ​bracing. You ‌do not ​appease ‌winter, and ​you do ‌not wait ​it out ‌in reverent ​silence; you ​make a ‌doll of ‌it, carry ‌it to ​the river ​in procession, ‌singing, ​and hold ​it under. ‌Renewal is ​not a ​mood but ‌an act ​— an ‌act with ​a body ​count of ​one, gladly ​paid. ‌There is ‌also a ​darker reading ‌available. The ​effigy is ​a woman, ‌and the ‌village drowns ‌her so ‌the crops ​can grow. ‌However we ​judge ​that image, ​the ritual ‌holds it ​up every ​spring and ​lets us ‌look. Perhaps ​that is ​the deepest ​use of ‌Marzanna: a ​culture ‌keeping, in ​public and ‌with its ​children watching, ‌a ceremony ‌that admits ​winter must ​be killed ​— and ​asks who, ‌each year, ‌does the ​killing.[^1]
